title: the summit sit
hook: a king finally sits down to eat after a long fast, and the guests keep coming

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit laid the schools of thought side by side, each one a way of seeing, none on top. Did you ask how you knew, before answering a message? Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

The plate is finally in front of him. King Rantideva and his family have gone without food for a long time, and now there's a little rice, a little ghee, some water. He lifts his hand to eat. There's a knock. A guest, hungry. The king shares. Another knock. Another guest. He shares again. Then a man arrives with his dogs, all of them hungry. Today's summit sit climbs back to the lineage track, and the stretch on karma and seva: work, and work given away.
screen: `THE PLATE, FINALLY.` → `A KNOCK. ANOTHER KNOCK.` → `WORK, GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's how the Bhagavata finishes the story, in paraphrase. The king gives the man with the dogs everything that's left, and bows to him and to the dogs. Only the water is left now. Then one more person comes, an outcaste by the rules of the day, thirsty, asking for a drink. The king gives him the water. And as he does, he says something. He doesn't want great powers from God, he says, and he doesn't even ask to be freed from rebirth. He asks to enter into the sorrow of all beings and carry it, so that they can be free of it. Then the story turns: the guests were gods who had come to test him. They show themselves, and he asks them for nothing. Hold that next to the other stretches of the track. In the Uddhava Gita, a wandering beggar has his bowl snatched away, and he blames no one, not people, not the gods, not even karma, only the grip of his own mind. In the Gita, Krishna says the true renouncer isn't the one who quits his work and lets the fire go out. It's the one who does the work that needs doing, without leaning on what it brings back. And then seva: service, offered as worship. Put together, from up here, the lineage track's first stretch says something simple and hard. Karma isn't just a ledger of what comes back to you. It's work done without clutching the result. And seva is what that work looks like when the result goes to someone else. Rantideva's plate is the picture of it. The meal was his. It ended up feeding a guest, a stranger, a man with dogs, and a thirsty outcaste, and when the gods stood in front of him, he had nothing left to ask for.
screen: `THE LAST OF THE WATER, GIVEN.` · `THE BOWL SNATCHED, NO ONE BLAMED.` · `DO THE WORK, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.` · `SEVA: WORK WHOSE FRUIT GOES TO ANOTHER.` · then, large: `NOTHING LEFT TO ASK FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the work in your hands. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one piece of work you'll do today, something ordinary: a shift, a meal, a report, a ride you're giving someone. See yourself doing it well. Then, on an out-breath, let your shoulders drop, as if setting down what it will bring you: the thanks, the credit, the result. Keep the work. Let the fruit go. Breathe like that. If you pray, you can offer the work to God before you begin. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: karma and seva, work done without clutching, and a king who gave away his last cup of water. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, do one small job whose fruit goes to someone else, and don't mention it. Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Hindus practice seva in many forms: cooking and serving food at temples, caring for the sick and elderly, or working in the community, offered as service to God rather than for reward.

original.note: Sanskrit and Hindi, in Devanagari: sevā, service, offered as worship.

trapdoor: what you thought: seva means volunteering.
what it means: it's service offered as worship, work whose fruit goes to someone else.
what a scholar hears: Rantideva in Bhagavata 9.21, giving away his last food and water, read beside Gita 6.1 on the renouncer who keeps working without leaning on the fruit.

notes: Summit sit, day 6: revisits the lineage track's 'karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita' (1202–1207) and 'seva as vocation' (1208–1213). Rantideva also appeared on 1210; this day retells the ending (the water and his words) at more length.

Rantideva, Bhagavata 9.21, paraphrased: after a long fast, food arrives; he gives to a brahmin guest, a shudra guest, a man with dogs, and finally water to a pulkasa (outcaste). His words: he does not seek the eightfold powers or release from rebirth, but to enter into all beings and bear their suffering. The length of the fast is not stated in the voice. 'An outcaste by the rules of the day' is the script's framing; confirm it is acceptable.
The mendicant of Avanti (Bhagavata 11.23): blames neither people, gods, planets, karma nor time, but the mind. Confirm.
Gita 6.1 paraphrased (not the one without fire and without action). Confirm.

Editor pass: the Rantideva ending now follows Bhagavata 9.21 (the guests reveal themselves as gods; he asks nothing) instead of 'leaves him with an empty plate … his whole reward'; the Avanti mendicant is no longer called 'old'; the practice's open-palms gesture, close to 1409's open hand, changed to dropping the shoulders.
